tier_reason: PR #2915 publishes the benchmark code (benchmark/benchmark_numpy.cpp, benchmark/CMakeLists.txt, tools/report_numpy_benchmarks.py) with -O3 -march=native flags, but the reported run states neither the compiler nor the CPU model (only host 'Quantstacklaptopalexis', CPU scaling on), and the numbers are first-party from an unmerged contributor PR, so it cannot be A.

corrections.workload: 46 NumPy-comparable functions (elementwise math such as sin, cos, tan, sinh, hypot, add, multiply, and reducers sum/mean/amin/amax/prod over all elements or one axis) on square 2D float64 arrays of 64x64 and 512x512 (Google Benchmark Range(64, 512)), single-threaded (OMP/OpenBLAS/MKL thread env vars set to 1); xtensor writes into a preallocated result via xt::noalias, NumPy is called from the same C++ executable through embedded Python with out= into the same buffer, Google Benchmark cpu_time, ratio = NumPy time / xtensor time (geomean over the two sizes).
corrections.caveats: (1) Numbers come from an open, unmerged pull request (#2915, 'Add comparative benchmarks with numpy', opened 2026-05-13, ready for review 2026-05-18, no reviews) by xtensor contributor Alex-PLACET; the merged benchmark/ directory has no NumPy, Eigen or BLAS comparison and no published results (benchmark_stl.cpp only compares xtensor with std::transform). (2) Single laptop run, two sizes (64x64 and 512x512) per function, CPU model and compiler of that run not stated, CPU scaling and ASLR enabled. (3) NumPy is built from source with unpinned version; every NumPy timing includes the embedded-Python PyObject_Call overhead, which inflates small (64x64) ratios for cheap ops; the harness has no check that xtensor/xsimd and NumPy produce the same values (accuracy of xsimd transcendental approximations is not compared). (4) Mixed result: xtensor faster on 34 of 46 functions, NumPy faster on 10 (exp, exp2, cosh, amax_all, amin_all and the axis-0 reductions sum/mean/amin/amax/prod; prod_axis0 at 512x512 is 11.6x slower in xtensor), 2 level (round, sum_all). (5) The category's baseline Eigen is not beaten: README says only that statically dimensioned performance 'matches' Eigen (no numbers), and the independent ros-navigation/navigation2 issue #4237 ('[MPPI]: Replace xtensor with Eigen Experiment') reports Eigen faster (2000x60 dot product 5.36 ms xtensor vs 0.76 ms Eigen; MPPI BM_DiffDrive 11.56 vs 8.58 ms on an 8th-gen i7 with AVX2; ROS1 control loop on an i5-12400F level at 5 ms average), compiler not stated. (6) The separate xtensor-benchmark repo (xtensor vs Eigen3, Armadillo, Blitz++) publishes no result numbers. (7) Category fit is loose: elementwise math and reductions, not BLAS/LAPACK kernels.

notes: Numbers in claimed_speedup match the PR #2915 summary table exactly (hypot 3.85x, tan 3.76x, cos 2.85x, sinh 4.95x with 165511 vs 1560352 ns at 512, atanh 2.36x, prod_axis0 0.39x with 632740 vs 54496 ns, mean_axis0 0.58x, amax_axis0 0.47x, cosh 0.70x, round 1.01x, sum_all 1.05x; 34/10/2 split). Harness is sound (xtensor result forced via noalias assignment and DoNotOptimize, NumPy writes to a preallocated out buffer) but includes Python call overhead on the NumPy side and no result check; shortcomings: unmerged first-party PR, no CPU/compiler, slower than NumPy on axis-0 reductions and slower than Eigen per navigation2 #4237. tier_reason: The only numbers are a CI run of flatironinstitute/web-wavelets-benchmarking (src/benchmark.ts, by the authors of the wasmlets wrapper) comparing wavelib-in-WebAssembly with a pure-JS package and PyWavelets under Pyodide; code and emcc flags (-O3 --closure 1 in the wasmlets Makefile) are public, but the runner CPU model and emcc version are not stated and it is not a well-known suite, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: wavedec vs discrete-wavelets (pure JS): 100000 db2 1.28 vs 162.48 ms (~127x, derived from page data); 100000 db4 2.27 vs 185.34 ms (~82x derived); 1000000 db2 13.19 vs 2030.32 ms (~154x derived); 1000000 db4 22.94 vs 2572.65 ms (~112x derived); discrete-wavelets has no waverec result (N/A). Against PyWavelets in Pyodide (data kept in Python memory) wasmlets decomposition is slower in all four cases (1.28 vs 1.23, 2.27 vs 1.64, 13.19 vs 10.16, 22.94 vs 14.93 ms; PyWavelets 1.5x faster on 1M db4), while reconstruction is faster in three of four (0.77 vs 1.20, 1.30 vs 1.41, 8.85 vs 9.70 ms) and slower on 1M db4 (15.18 vs 12.88 ms). Against PyWavelets with per-trial JS/Python marshalling, wasmlets is faster in every case (e.g. 1.28 vs 4.95 ms dec, 0.77 vs 4.94 ms rec at 100000 db2).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Emscripten (emcc) build of wavelib via the wasmlets Makefile with CFLAGS -O3 --closure 1 (emcc version not pinned or stated). Benchmark harness is TypeScript on Node.js 18 in GitHub Actions; PyWavelets comes from pyodide ^0.25.0; wasmlets ^0.0.6 in package.json.

notes: Numbers on benchmark.md match the record for the discrete-wavelets comparison; the PyWavelets comparison was slightly overstated as 'no win' (wasmlets wins 3 of 4 reconstruction rows and all marshalling rows) and is corrected. Shortcomings for the orchestrator: no FFTW or other native-library comparison exists; the only win is against a small pure-JS npm package; the measured artefact is the wasmlets WebAssembly wrapper, not native wavelib; fCWT README (MacBook Pro 2019 i9) shows wavelib slowest of all CWT implementations (100k-3000: 45.04 s vs PyWavelets 12.69 s); category 'fft' is a loose fit (wavelet transforms).
